Article Title: Is Pakistan facilitating Chinese missile shipments to Iran? Islamabad responds
Article Text:
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir (AP file photo)

Pakistan has pushed back strongly against reports claiming it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran, as Tehran remains locked in a tense standoff with the Donald Trump-led US administration.The rejection by Munir's military comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington, exposing its two-faced tendency in its foreign policy approach.Pakistan’s military chief has recently found favour with US President Donald Trump , while Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.Reacting to reports that Pakistan was set to facilitate the transit of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defence missile systems to Iran, the Trump's "favourite field marshal"-led army dismissed the claims outright.“All such speculations are baseless and devoid of truth,” Pakistan’s military media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, according to Azerbaijan news, citing Anadolu Agency.“Such speculations are categorically rejected,” the ISPR added.The denial came after Reuters reported on Wednesday that Iran was expected to receive its first shipment of Chinese air defence systems within weeks, as Tehran looks to rebuild its defensive capabilities amid its conflict with the United States.According to Reuters, the initial deliveries were planned to move from Urumqi in western China and pass through Pakistan before reaching Iran, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. The sources, however, did not clarify whether the transit would take place by air or through land routes.The reports emerged amid speculation over US weapons stockpiles being stretched due to ongoing global conflicts, though Trump later dismissed such concerns. The episode has once again highlighted Islamabad’s delicate balancing act between Beijing and Washington as tensions continue to rise around Iran.
Article Summary: Pakistan denies reports it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran. Comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington. Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.

Article Title: This Swiss town will fine dog owners who do not wash away their pets' urine from streets and building facades
Article Text:
Why Chiasso fining dog owners for not washing away their pets' urine?



What does the new rule require?



What are the penalties for breaking the rule?

Is this the first rule of its kind in Switzerland?



Could other towns follow Chiasso's example?

Dog owners visiting the Swiss border town of Chiasso will soon have one more responsibility besides picking up after their pets. From mid-August 2026, anyone whose dog urinates on pavements or building facades in the town centre must rinse the area with water or risk a fine for repeat offences. The unusual regulation, believed to be the first of its kind in Switzerland, was introduced after residents complained about persistent foul odours caused by dog urine, particularly during hot and dry summer weather. Officials say the measure is intended to improve public hygiene, preserve the appearance of public spaces and encourage greater civic responsibility rather than punish pet owners. The move has attracted global attention for extending clean-up duties beyond solid waste.Chiasso, located in Switzerland's southern canton of Ticino near the Italian border, introduced the new by-law after receiving numerous complaints about unpleasant smells in the town centre. Authorities said dog urine left on pavements and building facades had become a growing nuisance, especially during prolonged periods of hot, dry weather when there was little rain to naturally wash away the residue. With around 500 registered dogs in the town, officials believe the measure will help improve hygiene and make public spaces cleaner and more pleasant for residents and visitors alike.Under the regulation, dog owners must carry a bottle or container of water while walking their pets through Chiasso's town centre. If a dog urinates on a pavement or building facade, the owner is expected to immediately rinse or dilute the urine with water. The requirement applies specifically to public areas covered by the municipal by-law and complements the existing obligation to pick up dog faeces.The municipality has adopted a warning-first approach. Anyone caught violating the rule for the first time will receive a warning instead of an immediate penalty. However, repeat offenders can be fined 100 Swiss francs (CHF 100), equivalent to about $122. Municipal police will enforce the regulation during their regular patrols, with officials hoping education and public awareness will encourage compliance before fines become necessary.According to Chiasso officials, yes. While municipalities across Switzerland already require dog owners to collect and properly dispose of dog waste, Chiasso is believed to be the first to introduce a rule specifically requiring owners to rinse away dog urine from streets and building facades. The measure has already sparked interest from other municipalities, with nearby Locarno reportedly considering a similar policy if Chiasso's initiative proves successful.The regulation has gone viral because it expands the traditional responsibilities of pet owners beyond cleaning up solid waste. Many social media users were surprised that dog owners may now have to carry water bottles specifically to rinse away urine, while others praised the town's efforts to improve cleanliness and reduce unpleasant odours. The story has also sparked wider conversations about responsible pet ownership, public hygiene and how cities can better maintain shared urban spaces.Although it remains too early to know whether the policy will spread widely, Chiasso's approach has already generated discussion in other parts of Switzerland. Officials maintain that the objective is not to discourage dog ownership but to encourage residents to take greater responsibility for shared public areas. If the initiative successfully reduces complaints and improves cleanliness, similar regulations could eventually be considered by other towns facing the same problem.
Article Summary: Chiasso introduced the new by-law after receiving numerous complaints about unpleasant smells in the town centre. If a dog urinates on a pavement or building facade, the owner is expected to immediately rinse or dilute the urine with water. Repeat offenders can be fined 100 Swiss francs (CHF 100), equivalent to about $122.

Article Title: Billionaire Mark Zuckerberg had quietly bought another Lake Tahoe estate. Inside his growing $100 million-plus property empire
Article Text:
Palo Alto properties

All in, he shelled out over $43 million to stitch together his private slice of Palo Alto, now spread over 1.83 acres—a walled garden of tech, tranquillity, and very expensive real estate.

Hawaii holdings

Lake Tahoe compound

D.C. Mansion

In March 2025, the social media mogul plunked down $23 million in cash for a striking 15,400-square-foot mansion

Miami beach estate

San Francisco pied-à-terre

When you have money, you develop hobbies and preferences that are different from the layman. While a millionaire could have a thing for collecting watches, a billionaire could be into buying up yachts. When it comes to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg , he has a propensity for large compounds. The billionaire tech giant with a net worth of more than $200 billion doesn't just buy a house, he buys the whole block. From a sprawling compound in Hawaii to a San Francisco pied-à-terre, he has a property portfolio that would make others in his league shy of their own choices, according to a report by Robb Report.Mark Zuckerberg is the one you should look up to for a masterclass in billionaire nesting. The Facebook founder's primary residence in Palo Alto is less of a single home and more of a meticulously curated mini compound, the result of a series of strategic purchases aimed at preserving privacy and control over the immediate surroundings.In March 2011, he bought a 5,617-square-foot home on Edgewood Drive for $7 million. Just 10 minutes from the social media platform’s Menlo Park HQ, the five-bedroom, five-and-a-half-bath residence came with a saltwater pool, a glass-enclosed sunroom, and a sprawling backyard pavilion.In 2012, he acquired a neighbouring three-bedroom, three-bath home for $4.8 million, and the following year he doubled down—scooping up two additional residences for a combined $10.5 million in September and a four-bedroom abode in October for a cool $14.5 million. While Zuckerberg wanted to demolish all four of the homes and create one seamless compound, the city nixed his demolition proposal in 2016, per CNBC. Instead, the tech mogul opted for renovations, reportedly leasing the properties back to their original owners in the meantime. All in, he shelled out over $43 million to stitch together his private slice of Palo Alto, now spread over 1.83 acres—a walled garden of tech, tranquillity, and very expensive real estate.Zuckerberg's real estate ambitions are not limited to Silicon Valley or San Francisco, they stretched all the way to Kauai in the form of a private estate. He began his aloha chapter in 2014, when he quietly purchased two lush parcels on Kauai’s North Shore: the 357-acre Kahu’aina Plantation (a former sugarcane farm) for around $66 million and a majority stake in a 393-acre Pila’a Beach spread for roughly $49.8 million. Combined, the two properties total more than 700 acres and set him back about $116 million. That figure has since ballooned. In 2025, he added another 962 acres of ranchland, spending over $65 million, according to Wired.The estate, now known as Koʻolau Ranch, is as extravagant as it is elusive. There are two sprawling mansions clocking in at around 57,000 square feet combined, with 30 bedrooms and 30 bathrooms, an industrial kitchen, conference rooms, multiple elevators, and a tunnel that leads to a 5,000-square-foot underground shelter complete with an escape hatch and bomb-shelter-style doors. Zuckerberg has downplayed the bunker rumours, describing it as “a little shelter,” but the intrigue remains. According to new permits, Zuckerberg is adding three more large-scale structures to the property, each spanning between 7,800 and 11,000 square feet—roughly ten times the size of a typical Hawaiian home. Two of them are dorm-style lodges, each outfitted with 16 bedrooms, 16 bathrooms, and a shared 1,300-square-foot lanai. The price tag? Between $3.5 million and $4 million apiece.In classic Zuckerberg fashion, the 42-year-old scooped up two neighbouring estates totalling about 10 acres on the pristine west shore of the lake, one in December 2018 for $22 million and the others a few weeks later for $37 million. The first of the two, the storied Carousel Estate, sits on 3.5 acres and boasts 200 feet of lake frontage, a private marina-style pier, and enough towering old-growth trees to make it feel like your own national park. At the time he acquired it, the estate included an eight-bedroom main house, a three-bedroom guesthouse, and a caretaker’s apartment. It has since been torn down to make way for something far more grand, SFGate has reported.Next door, the Brushwood Estate brought another six acres to the party, with 400 feet of shoreline and a private pier. This was no sleepy Tahoe lodge and once hosted glitzy soirées like an Oscar de la Renta fashion show and the Lake Tahoe Summer Music Festival.Both properties are being transformed into what planning documents describe as a seven-building compound designed to blend rustic elegance with cutting-edge luxury. At the heart of it all is a 20,000-square-foot, 35-foot-tall main residence, shaped like an L, clad in timber and glass, and crowned with a shingled roof.While a surprising choice, this real estate choice is situated in the heart of the nation's capital, where numerous other billionaires have been flocking since the 2024 election. In March 2025, the social media mogul plunked down $23 million in cash for a striking 15,400-square-foot mansion in the exclusive Massachusetts Avenue Heights neighbourhood, making it one of the top three most expensive residential sales in the district’s history. The purchase was wrapped in secrecy but eventually confirmed by Meta, which said the home would allow Zuckerberg to “spend more time [in D.C.] as Meta continues the work on policy issues related to American technology leadership.” Designed by renowned architect Robert Gurney, the residence has been hailed for a classic elegance with a clean and modern aesthetic.Tell us one tech CEO who doesn't have an estate in Miami, it almost comes expected with the Silicon Valley resume. In 2026, Mark Zuckerberg and his wife were widely rumoured to be expanding their already formidable real estate portfolio to Miami’s ultra-exclusive Indian Creek Island, the guard-gated enclave known as the “Billionaire Bunker.”Zuckerberg and Chan have closed on a sprawling waterfront compound at 7 Indian Creek Island Road for $170 million, setting a new residential sales record in Miami-Dade County. The nearly 28,000-square-foot estate sits on roughly two acres with about 200 feet of Biscayne Bay frontage and was developed by cosmetic surgeon Dr. Aaron Rollins and his wife, real estate agent Marine Rollins. Designed by Ferris Rafauli, the residence has a private resort, a jazz lounge and hidden-passage library to a spa suite, aquarium-lined living spaces and a yacht-ready dock.He briefly owned a renovated SF pied-à-terre, which he later sold for around $31 million after a multimillion-dollar glow-up.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg is the one you should look up to for a masterclass in billionaire nesting. The Facebook founder's primary residence in Palo Alto is less of a single home and more of a meticulously curated mini compound. In March 2025, he plunked down $23 million in cash for a striking 15,400-square-foot mansion in Miami.

Article Title: An ancient Mexican city once home to 90,000 people vanished nearly 1,000 years ago. Scientists think a 650-year drought may explain why
Article Text:
PC: UC Berkeley News

The volcanic landscape behind Cantona's remarkable growth

PC: AI Generated

Lake sediments reveal centuries of drought in ancient Mexico

How drought and politics shaped Cantona's rise and fall

How repeated drought strained Cantona's food supply

Why drought was not the only reason Cantona was abandoned

“We can show that both the growth and

decline of the site took place during a time period of frequent drought, which forces us to think in more nuanced ways about how political and social factors interact with environmental factors to cause social and cultural change,”

. “

A wider picture of ancient Mesoamerica

Around a thousand years ago, the ancient city of Cantona stood as one of the largest urban centres in the Americas, with an estimated population of 90,000 people. Built on the volcanic highlands of central Mexico, the fortified settlement thrived for centuries before it was mysteriously abandoned by the mid-11th century. Archaeologists have long debated what caused its decline, pointing to conflict, political upheaval and shifting trade networks. The PNAS study suggests climate may have played a crucial role. By analysing sediments from a nearby lake, scientists uncovered evidence of a prolonged 650-year period of recurring drought that coincided with Cantona's final centuries. While researchers say drought alone did not doom the city, the findings offer fresh insight into how environmental stress combined with social and political pressures may have led to its eventual collapse.According to the study, Cantona occupied a striking position within the Cuenca Oriental, a high-altitude basin in central Mexico known for its dry climate and volcanic landscape. Although the environment was never especially forgiving, the area offered one valuable advantage: rich deposits of obsidian, the volcanic glass that served as one of the most important raw materials in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica.The city appears to have grown into a major centre for both trade and regional defence.Reportedly, archaeological evidence suggests it may have housed around 90,000 inhabitants during its height, making it one of the largest settlements in the New World before European contact. Its heavily fortified design also hints at a landscape shaped by political uncertainty rather than prolonged peace.The PNAS study titled, ‘ Cultural implications of late Holocene climate change in the Cuenca Oriental, Mexico ’ revealed that instead of relying solely on archaeological remains, scientists turned to the sediments preserved beneath Lake Aljojuca. Fine layers of mud, minerals and organic material settled year after year, quietly recording changes in the surrounding environment.The research team examined oxygen isotope patterns locked within carbonate deposits. These chemical signatures shift depending on the balance between rainfall and evaporation, making them useful indicators of wetter or drier conditions. Radiocarbon dating of organic material within the sediments allowed the timeline of environmental change to be reconstructed over many centuries.Their analysis pointed towards a long interval of recurring drought that stretched from around AD 500 until approximately AD 1150. Rather than a single catastrophic event, the record suggests repeated periods of reduced rainfall over roughly 650 years, as reported by the UC Berkeley News. The findings also fit into an even broader trend indicating that parts of Mexico's highlands had been gradually becoming drier since around 200 BC before conditions began improving again during the early 14th century.One aspect of the evidence stands out because it does not follow the simplest explanation. Cantona did not immediately shrink when rainfall became less reliable. Instead, its population appears to have expanded during the earlier stages of the prolonged dry spell.This pattern suggests climate alone cannot explain the city's fortunes. Political changes elsewhere may have driven people towards Cantona, whose defensive layout and strategic position along important inland routes could have made it a comparatively secure destination. At roughly the same time, the influential city of Teotihuacan, located further west, was itself experiencing decline.Only after centuries of repeated dry conditions does the picture begin to change. By around AD 1050, long-term environmental pressure may have weakened local farming and water supplies enough to make continued occupation increasingly difficult.Agriculture in the Cuenca Oriental was already constrained by geography. Modern farming without irrigation sits close to the northern limit for successful maize cultivation, suggesting ancient communities were operating with little margin for prolonged shortages of rainfall.The climate itself did not transform into a desert overnight. Seasonal rainfall patterns probably continued much as before, with summer monsoons followed by dry winters. The difference appears to have been the increasing frequency of shorter drought episodes, each placing additional strain on crops, water storage and local food production.Communities can often absorb isolated poor harvests. Repeated failures over generations create a different challenge altogether, particularly for a large urban population dependent on surrounding farmland.According to UC Berkeley News, geography graduate student Tripti Bhattacharya and professor Roger Byrne states that the climate record does not argue that drought single-handedly brought about Cantona's abandonment. Instead, it supports a more complicated sequence in which environmental stress interacts with existing political and social changes.Bhattacharya saidThe city's expansion during the early centuries of the dry period makes that clear. If climate alone determined events, growth would be difficult to explain. The evidence instead points towards a settlement that benefited from wider regional instability before eventually facing mounting ecological pressures that became increasingly difficult to overcome.Cantona is only one example among many archaeological sites where drought has been proposed as part of the explanation for societal change. Across Mesoamerica, researchers continue to investigate whether prolonged shifts in rainfall affected different regions at different times, rather than triggering a single continent-wide crisis.Large gaps remain in the prehistoric climate record for Mexico's central highlands, making studies based on lake sediments especially valuable. By combining archaeological evidence with environmental records, scientists are gradually building a clearer picture of how ancient communities adapted, reorganised or relocated when faced with long-term changes in water availability.
Article Summary: Cantona stood as one of the largest urban centres in the Americas, with an estimated population of 90,000 people. Built on the volcanic highlands of central Mexico, the fortified settlement thrived for centuries before it was mysteriously abandoned by the mid-11th century. By analysing sediments from a nearby lake, scientists uncovered evidence of a prolonged 650-year period of recurring drought.

Article Title: In 1995 Yellowstone began bringing back wolves; 30 years later young aspens returned, but the wider recovery remains uneven
Article Text:
Representative image of wolves in Yellowstone National Park (AI-generated)

What happened after Yellowstone lost its wolves

Study found new trees in stands that had been suppressed for decades

New research warns against declaring a park-wide recovery

Rising bison numbers may create another challenge

Three decades after wolves returned to Yellowstone National Park, young aspen trees are growing tall in parts of the park’s northern range for the first time in generations. The change has added fresh evidence to one of conservation’s best-known stories, but scientists say the results are more complicated than the popular version suggests.The United States began restoring wolves to Yellowstone in January 1995. Fourteen animals from Canada were brought to the park that year, followed by 17 more in 1996. In total, 31 wolves were relocated during the two-year programme. It was the first deliberate attempt to return a large predator to such a vast ecosystem in the country.The return of wolves changed how predators and prey interacted across Yellowstone. Elk numbers declined, while bears and cougars also played a part in increasing pressure on the herds. With fewer elk feeding on young trees in some areas, aspen shoots finally had a better chance of growing beyond the height at which they could be eaten.Wolves were once common in Yellowstone, but government predator-control programmes and hunting pushed them towards extinction in the park. Between 1914 and 1926, at least 136 wolves were killed there. By the 1940s, established packs had almost disappeared, and a survey in the 1970s found no evidence of a resident population.During the decades without wolves, Yellowstone’s elk population grew and placed heavy pressure on aspen, willow and other vegetation. Elk repeatedly ate young shoots before they could become trees. Old aspens remained standing, but few young ones survived to replace them.This decline affected more than the trees. Aspen stands provide food and shelter for beavers, insects and birds, including species that nest inside holes in older trunks. When the trees struggled to regenerate, the habitat they created also began to disappear.The wolf restoration programme was not designed only to save aspens. Its main purpose was to restore a native predator that had been removed by humans. But researchers were interested in whether bringing back wolves would create wider changes across the food web. A 2025 study examined 87 aspen stands across Yellowstone’s northern range. Researchers found large numbers of tall saplings across about one-third of the stands. Another third contained smaller patches of young trees that were beginning to join the overstory. The remaining stands were still being held back by grazing animals.The researchers described the growth as the first new generation of overstory aspens recorded in the area in around 80 years. Surveys conducted during the 1990s had found no comparable group of tall young trees in the stands examined.Lead researcher Luke Painter said the restoration of large carnivores had restarted a recovery process that had been blocked for decades. The stands with many tall saplings also had lower rates of browsing, while trees in other areas were still being heavily eaten.This pattern supports the idea of a trophic cascade. The term describes a process in which changes involving predators at the top of a food web affect animals and plants below them.In Yellowstone, wolves did not directly help the aspens. Instead, they preyed on elk and contributed to changes in elk numbers and behaviour. That reduced pressure on young trees in some locations, allowing them to grow.The signs of new growth do not mean every aspen stand in Yellowstone is recovering. study being presented at the Ecological Society of America’s 2026 annual meeting is titled “Persistent landscape-scale aspen decline following large carnivore restoration in northern Yellowstone National Park.” The research is led by Dan MacNulty of Utah State University and includes scientists from Utah State and the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point.The presentation brings attention back to the scale at which recovery is measured. A group of stands can contain many new trees even while the wider landscape continues to lose older aspens. Local recovery and a broader decline can happen at the same time.Scientists have debated this issue for years. Earlier research found that elk did not always avoid aspen stands in places where the risk of meeting wolves was higher. This challenged the simple idea that fear alone caused elk to leave certain valleys and allowed trees to return.The National Park Service also describes the relationship between wolves, elk and vegetation as complex. Yellowstone contains several large predators, including wolves, bears and cougars. Elk numbers are also affected by weather, food availability and hunting outside the park. The effect of wolves can therefore differ from one part of the ecosystem to another.Elk are not the only animals that eat young aspens. Researchers say Yellowstone’s growing bison population may now be limiting tree recovery in some areas.Bison can feed on young shoots and sometimes break saplings while moving through or browsing inside aspen stands. This means a tree that is no longer being heavily eaten by elk may still struggle to survive because of pressure from another large herbivore.Conditions such as drought, soil quality, fires and the location of individual stands can also affect growth. Trees near water or in productive soil may recover more easily than those growing in dry or exposed places.These factors help explain why some parts of northern Yellowstone now contain tall young aspens while others remain largely unchanged.Thirty years after wolves returned, the evidence shows that the animals helped reshape Yellowstone. They restored a missing predator, affected elk populations and created conditions that allowed aspens to grow in some locations.But the recovery did not happen everywhere, and wolves did not act alone. Yellowstone’s changing forest is the result of several predators, herbivores, climate conditions and local habitats interacting over decades.The young aspens are an important sign of progress. They are not proof that every part of the ecosystem has returned to its earlier state.
Article Summary: Wolves were once common in Yellowstone, but government predator-control programmes and hunting pushed them towards extinction in the park. Between 1914 and 1926, at least 136 wolves were killed there. By the 1940s, established packs had almost disappeared, and a survey in the 1970s found no evidence of a resident population.

Article Title: Millions of birds follow a 9,000-kilometre invisible highway every year, crossing mountains, deserts and oceans without a map
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

A migration route that crosses mountains, deserts and oceans

Home to some of the world's highest bird migrations

Why protecting the flyway matters

Every year, as the seasons change, millions of birds undertake one of nature's greatest journeys. Some travel only a few hundred kilometres, while others fly thousands without recognising political borders or national boundaries. Instead, they follow ancient migration routes known as flyways, natural aerial corridors shaped by geography, climate and the availability of food and resting sites.One of the world's most important of these routes is the Central Asian Flyway (CAF). Spanning around 9,000 kilometres, it connects the breeding grounds of northern Eurasia with the wetlands, forests, grasslands and coastlines of South Asia. Supporting hundreds of migratory bird species across 30 countries, the flyway has become a vital lifeline for birds travelling between Europe, Asia and the Indian Ocean each year.The Central Asian Flyway stretches from the Arctic Ocean and Siberia southwards through Central Asia before reaching countries including India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and the Maldives.Rather than following a single narrow path, the flyway consists of a network of interconnected habitats where birds can rest, feed and breed during different stages of their migration. These include high-altitude lakes on the Tibetan Plateau, the wetlands of Kazakhstan, India's floodplains, coastal estuaries and mangrove forests.According to the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) , the flyway supports more than 600 migratory bird species, including cranes, geese, ducks, shorebirds, raptors and songbirds. Many of these species depend on the same chain of wetlands and stopover sites every year, making the health of each habitat critical to the success of their migration.One of the flyway's most remarkable features is that it includes the migration route of the bar-headed goose, a bird famous for flying over the Himalayas, where it has been recorded at altitudes exceeding 7,000 metres. At these heights, oxygen levels are only a fraction of those at sea level, yet the species has evolved specialised lungs, efficient blood circulation and powerful muscles that allow it to survive one of the most demanding migrations on Earth.Other iconic migrants using the Central Asian Flyway include the Siberian crane, greater flamingo, Amur falcon, black-tailed godwit and numerous species of ducks and waders that winter across the Indian subcontinent.Researchers continue to study these migrations using satellite tracking, GPS transmitters and bird-ringing programmes, revealing increasingly detailed maps of the remarkable journeys birds undertake every year.Because migratory birds rely on multiple countries during a single journey, conserving the Central Asian Flyway requires international cooperation. Wetland destruction, pollution, climate change, illegal hunting and habitat fragmentation threaten many of the stopover sites birds depend upon to rest and refuel.Recognising these challenges, countries across the region have worked together through the Central Asian Flyway Action Plan, developed under the Convention on Migratory Species, to improve habitat conservation, strengthen scientific monitoring and coordinate protection efforts across national borders.Scientists emphasise that safeguarding the flyway benefits far more than birds alone. Healthy wetlands help reduce flooding, improve water quality, store carbon and support fisheries and local livelihoods. Protecting this vast aerial highway therefore preserves not only one of the world's greatest wildlife spectacles but also ecosystems that millions of people depend upon every day.
Article Summary: The Central Asian Flyway (CAF) connects the breeding grounds of northern Eurasia with the wetlands, forests, grasslands and coastlines of South Asia. Supporting hundreds of migratory bird species across 30 countries, the flyway has become a vital lifeline for birds travelling between Europe, Asia and the Indian Ocean each year.

Article Title: Security forces’ crackdown, civil unrest continue in POK, 20 dead
Article Text:
File photo: PoK unrest

The situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir ( POK ) remains volatile amid mass civilian unrest, election-related violence, and heavy crackdowns by Pakistani security forces. According to sources, Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad.The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured.Amnesty International USA said that the disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot were consistent with Pakistani authorities’ “long history of unlawful violence against protesters”. “We urge the Pakistani authorities torestore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area,” it said.While security forces continue to maintain a heightened presence in Rawalakot, Muzaffarabad and other areas, sources said the possibility of additional protests remains high over the coming days because of declining public confidence in the political process.Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.

Article Title: Inside Spain's 'cannibal cave': Scientists thought only children were victims. New fossils reveal adults were also eaten by Homo antecessor
Article Text:
What researchers found in the new Gran Dolina excavation

Why earlier evidence pointed mainly to children

How scientists confirmed the cannibalism at Gran Dolina

What remains unknown about why Homo antecessor practised cannibalism

Why Gran Dolina remains central to understanding early human behaviour

New fossil discoveries at Gran Dolina cave in northern Spain show that cannibalism practised by an ancient human relative called Homo antecessor was not limited to children, as earlier evidence had suggested. Researchers recovered two dozen bones and teeth belonging to this now extinct species, which lived in Europe between roughly 1.2 million and 770,000 years ago, and found that many of the newly uncovered remains came from adults rather than the young, defenceless individuals identified in previous excavations. Several of the bone fragments carried cut marks consistent with the use of stone tools, adding fresh detail to what is already considered the oldest known evidence of cannibalism practised for nutritional reasons among human relatives.According to astatement from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, known by its Spanish acronym IPHES, the newly recovered remains include fragments of a skull, spine, arm and leg bones, along with three teeth belonging to several individuals. The bones were found at Gran Dolina, part of the wider Sierra de Atapuerca archaeological complex, a site recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage location for its exceptional record of early human evolution in Europe.The total number of individuals identified at Gran Dolina has now risen to at least 13, with roughly half of them adults. Palmira Saladié, a biological anthropologist at IPHES who coordinated the excavation, said in the institute's statement that the discovery of more adult individuals, some of whom also carry cut marks, shows that cannibalism at the site was not restricted to younger members of the group.For decades, most of the evidence of cannibalism uncovered at Gran Dolina came from the bones of infants and juveniles. A 2010 study on the site had suggested that younger individuals may have made easier targets, since children and juveniles from a rival group would have been simpler to capture and kill than adults. This pattern shaped much of the scientific understanding of Homo antecessor's cannibalistic behaviour for years.The newly excavated adult remains complicate that earlier picture. Andreu Ollé, an archaeologist at IPHES, said in the institute's statement that the increase in the number of individuals identified at the site, particularly the addition of more adults, allows researchers to understand this ancient population from a far more complete perspective than was previously possible.Evidence supporting cannibalism at the site extends well beyond the human bones themselves. According to IPHES, excavations at Gran Dolina have also uncovered an assemblage of stone tools made from flint, quartzite and sandstone, alongside animal bones from species including hyenas, beavers, deer, horses and rhinoceroses. The butchering techniques identified on these animal remains closely match the cut marks found on the human bones, suggesting the same tools and methods were used on both.Some of the human bones recovered from the site also carry human bite marks, which researchers consider some of the most reliable physical evidence that the bodies found at Gran Dolina were actually consumed rather than simply subjected to ritual defleshing or other practices that leave similar cut marks without clear evidence of eating.Despite decades of research confirming that cannibalism took place at Gran Dolina, the underlying reason for the practice remains unresolved. Researchers hope the newly discovered adult remains will help clarify whether the behaviour was driven primarily by nutritional necessity, conflict between rival groups, or some other social or cultural factor specific to Homo antecessor communities.Marina Mosquera, an archaeologist at IPHES, said in the institute's statement that excavation of this new area at Gran Dolina has only just begun, and that the initial results already point to considerable scientific potential for further discoveries. Researchers are now carrying out additional analysis on the recovered bones to explore questions around age-related differences in how cannibalism was practised, the number and duration of individual cannibalistic episodes, and the broader social organisation of Homo antecessor groups.Gran Dolina has produced some of the clearest and most extensively studied evidence of cannibalism among any early human relative, making it a key reference point for researchers studying violence, survival strategies and social structure among ancient hominin populations. The site's location within the broader Atapuerca complex, already significant for having yielded some of the earliest known human fossils in Western Europe, adds further weight to its role in reconstructing how early human relatives lived, competed and, in this case, treated members of their own species after death.As excavation of the newly identified area continues, researchers expect the growing collection of adult and juvenile remains from Gran Dolina to offer a considerably fuller picture of Homo antecessor than earlier, more limited fossil evidence allowed, deepening scientific understanding of one of the most striking and still only partially explained behaviours documented among humanity's ancient relatives.
Article Summary: New fossil discoveries at Gran Dolina cave in northern Spain show that cannibalism practised by Homo antecessor was not limited to children. Researchers recovered two dozen bones and teeth belonging to this now extinct species, which lived in Europe between roughly 1.2 million and 770,000 years ago. Several of the bone fragments carried cut marks consistent with the use of stone tools, adding fresh detail to what is already considered the oldest known evidence of cannibalism among human relatives.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Tiger Woods: "Talent is something you are born with, and a skill is something you…" - a lesson on why practice matters more than natural ability
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Tiger Woods (Getty Images)

Quote of the day by Tiger Woods

The deeper meaning of Tiger Wood’s quote

Why Woods himself is the perfect person to say this

Why skill keeps growing while talent stays roughly where it started

Why consistent practice tends to beat raw potential

Why repeating the basics is what actually builds mastery

Why mistakes end up teaching more than easy wins do

Why discipline tends to matter more than motivation

Other famous quotes by Tiger Woods



"No matter how good you get you can always get better, and that's the exciting part."

"Achievements on the golf course are not what matters, decency and honesty are what matter."

"Other golfers may outplay me from time to time, but they'll never outwork me."

"We all make decisions. But in the end, our decisions make us."

Why this quote is relevant

Watching a champion perform can make success look effortless, as though it were simply handed to a lucky few at birth. Tiger Woods pushed back on that idea directly. "Talent is something you are born with, and a skill is something you develop," he said. "99% of what you need to succeed in golf are skills." Talent might give someone a starting point. What actually determines how far they get is what they choose to practise and refine every single day after that, a lesson that Woods himself spent decades proving through his own extraordinarily disciplined career."Talent is something you are born with, and a skill is something you develop. 99% of what you need to succeed in golf are skills"Woods draws a clear line between two very different things. Talent is natural ability, something someone may already have from a young age. Skill is something earned, built up through repetition, discipline, learning from mistakes and steady, continuous improvement, none of which arrives automatically no matter how talented someone started out. Saying that 99% of golfing success comes from skill is Woods arguing that raw natural ability, on its own, is almost never enough.Even the most naturally gifted players still need thousands of hours refining the basics and correcting weaknesses. The quote shifts attention away from what someone was simply born with and toward what they can actually control through effort.Woods has been blunt about his own background in the past. "People don't understand that when I grew up, I was never the most talented," he said. "I was never the biggest. I was never the fastest. I certainly was never the strongest. The only thing I had was my work ethic, and that's been what has gotten me this far." That is not a modest exaggeration. It is exactly the same claim the main quote is making, just told from the inside.Across a career spanning decades, Woods has won 15 major championships and 82 PGA Tour events, a total that ties him for the most wins in PGA Tour history. His success was never built on natural ability alone. It came from relentless practice, physical conditioning, mental preparation and constant technical adjustment, and after multiple serious injuries and surgeries, he rebuilt his game more than once through exactly the same patience and hard work his quote describes, refusing to simply rely on the natural gifts everyone assumed had carried him this far already.Natural talent might give someone a real head start early on, but skill keeps developing for as long as someone keeps working on it. A gifted musician still practises scales every day. An experienced surgeon still keeps learning new techniques years into their career. Nearly every profession rewards people who keep improving long after their natural strengths have already become obvious to everyone. Skill, unlike raw talent, is cumulative. Every hour spent genuinely learning adds a little more competence, confidence and consistency to what came before it.Potential only actually means something once it gets developed. Plenty of people with real natural gifts never fully use them because they lean too heavily on simply being gifted. Others, starting from a far more ordinary place, end up surpassing them purely through years of consistent practice. Sport shows this pattern constantly. Athletes with disciplined training habits generally outperform equally talented rivals who never prepared properly. The same pattern shows up in business, education, music and almost everywhere else too.Mastery rarely arrives through one dramatic breakthrough. It usually comes from repeating simple actions until they become second nature. Professional golfers spend enormous amounts of time on short putts, bunker shots and basic swing mechanics, and those small, repeated improvements are ultimately what separate elite performers from everyone else. The same is true elsewhere. Pilots rehearse emergency procedures long before they might ever need one. Excellence usually comes from repetition rather than a sudden flash of inspiration.Developing any real skill involves failing along the way, missed shots, disappointing rounds, rejected ideas. All of that failure carries useful information for anyone actually paying attention to it. Woods has spoken about analysing his own poor rounds directly rather than ignoring them, treating every mistake as part of the learning process rather than something to brush past.Motivation rises and falls depending on the day. Discipline is what keeps someone practising even once the initial enthusiasm has faded. People who wait to feel inspired before doing the work tend to make patchy, inconsistent progress. People who simply build a routine keep improving steadily regardless of how motivated they happen to feel on any given day.Modern culture tends to celebrate sudden success while skipping past the years of preparation that actually produced it. Woods' quote is a useful reminder that lasting achievement is usually built through steady, consistent effort rather than natural talent on its own. Talent might open the very first door. Skill is what actually decides how far someone gets to go after that, whatever field they happen to be working in.
Article Summary: Tiger Woods' quote of the day: "99% of what you need to succeed in golf are skills" Woods argues that raw natural ability, on its own, is almost never enough. Skill is something earned, built up through repetition, discipline and learning from mistakes.

Article Title: US court convicts Salman Rushdie attacker of providing 'material support' to Hezbollah
Article Text:
Salman Rushdie stabbing: Attacker convicted on Hezbollah support, terror charges

NEW DELHI: A US man already serving a 25-year prison sentence for attempting to murder Indian-British author Salman Rushdie has been convicted on additional federal charges, including providing material support to the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah , the BBC reported.A federal jury in New York on Wednesday found Hadi Matar guilty of engaging in an act of transnational terrorism and providing material support to Hezbollah, which is designated as a terrorist organisation by the US, UK and several other countries.Prosecutors argued that Matar was driven by the 1989 fatwa issued by Iran's then-supreme leader calling for Rushdie's death, as well as a 2006 speech by a former Hezbollah leader urging that the fatwa be carried out.Rushdie testified during the trial, recounting how he was stabbed 15 times during the 2022 attack that left him partially blind in one eye. He credited a firefighter with helping save his life.Matar's lawyers argued the attack was not an act of terrorism, but the jury convicted him on both federal charges.He is already serving a 25-year sentence after being convicted of attempted murder in a New York state court and now faces the possibility of life imprisonment, the BBC reported.
Article Summary: Hadi Matar found guilty of engaging in an act of transnational terrorism and providing material support to Hezbollah. He is already serving a 25-year sentence after being convicted of attempted murder in a New York state court. He now faces the possibility of life imprisonment.

Article Title: In 2023, Tropical Storm Hilary struck Southern California; 22 juvenile great white sharks abandoned their San Diego nursery and returned after conditions improved
Article Text:
Great white sharks (Representative image)

A storm that changed the coast

Representative image

Why this nursery matters

What the researchers tracked

Where did they go?

Representative image

The role of cold water

Why this matters for climate change

A rare look at shark behaviour

The bigger picture

When Tropical Storm Hilary hit Southern California in August 2023, people on land were bracing for flooding, strong winds and record rainfall. Underwater, a group of young great white sharks off San Diego were reacting to the same storm in a very different way: they left their nursery habitat and moved into more sheltered waters before returning once conditions improved.A study from UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Shark Lab at California State University, Long Beach provides the first direct evidence of juvenile white sharks responding to an extreme weather event like this. Using acoustic tags to follow 22 sharks before, during and after the storm, researchers found that many temporarily abandoned the area as Hilary hit, then came back within days or weeks.Tropical Storm Hilary was a rare event for Southern California. It was the first tropical storm to directly affect the region this century, and although it weakened from a Category 4 hurricane before landfall, it still caused serious damage across the southwestern United States and parts of Mexico.On the ocean side, the storm brought a sudden drop in sea-surface temperature, rougher conditions and coastal flooding.For juvenile great whites, that created a fast-changing environment in a nursery zone they normally rely on for warmth, food and safety.Young white sharks in Southern California spend their early years in shallow coastal habitats where waters are calmer and warmer, and prey like stingrays and small fish are easier to find. One of the best-known nursery areas sits off Torrey Pines and Del Mar, where juveniles gather in summer and fall before eventually moving into adult habitats.That kind of nursery is important because it gives young sharks a better chance to grow without as much pressure from larger predators. But it also makes them vulnerable when the environment changes suddenly.To understand how Hilary affected the sharks, the team followed 22 juvenile great whites, 13 females and 9 males, that had already been fitted with acoustic transmitters. Two underwater receiver arrays recorded more than 524,000 detections, creating a detailed picture of shark movement through the storm.Before Hilary arrived, the nursery regularly held 16 to 19 tagged sharks per hour. During the storm, that number fell by about half, dropping to as few as eight. Most of the missing sharks returned shortly after the weather improved, and nearly all were back within three weeks. Only one shark left as the storm arrived and was never detected again in San Diego that year.The researchers could not trace every individual exactly, but they did notice a clear rise in detections around La Jolla Cove. That area is next to a submarine canyon, which gives sharks fast access to deeper water and may offer a more sheltered place during rough coastal conditions.One shark with a pressure sensor made the deepest dive recorded in the study, reaching 132 meters, or 433 feet, in La Jolla Canyon on the day the storm hit. That dive may have helped the shark get away from the turbulence near the surface.The scientists think some sharks may have used La Jolla Cove as a temporary refuge while others went elsewhere. In other words, they did not all respond the same way: just as animals, and people, often react differently when conditions become dangerous.One of the biggest clues came from the temperature shift. During Hilary, sea-surface temperatures in the nursery dropped from 20°C to 13.9°C (68°F to 57°F ) in less than 24 hours. That sharp cooling lined up closely with the sharks’ departure.Juvenile white sharks are regional endotherms, meaning they can regulate body temperature better than many fish. Adults tolerate cold water relatively well, but younger sharks are more sensitive to sudden temperature changes. The researchers believe the juveniles likely moved toward warmer water until conditions stabilised.This study is about one storm, but its implications are bigger than that. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, scientists need to know how marine species respond when ocean conditions shift quickly.That matters especially in California, where people and white sharks are increasingly using the same coastal waters. Better understanding shark behaviour during storms can help scientists and coastal managers make smarter decisions about conservation, recreation and safety.What makes this study stand out is that it captured a natural response in real time. The sharks were not reacting to a lab experiment or a routine seasonal change. They were responding to a major storm that altered their habitat almost overnight.Lead author Jack Elstner said the study offers the first direct evidence of storm-response behavior in white sharks. Co-author Chris Lowe added that the finding shows how some sharks sought shelter from the storm, while others did something different, much like humans do during extreme weather.Hurricane Hilary caused more than $900 million in damage in the United States and led the National Hurricane Center to issue its first-ever tropical storm warning for Southern California. For the sharks, it also served as a warning of another kind: even a protected nursery can become unstable when weather turns violent.The good news is that the sharks mostly came back. That suggests juvenile white sharks may be resilient enough to ride out short-term disruption, at least in this case. But the study also shows how quickly a nursery can be disturbed when ocean conditions change fast.
Article Summary: Tropical Storm Hilary hit Southern California in August 2023. The storm brought a sudden drop in sea-surface temperature, rougher conditions and coastal flooding. For juvenile great whites, that created a fast-changing environment in a nursery zone they normally rely on for warmth, food and safety. To understand how Hilary affected the sharks, the team followed 22 juvenileGreat whites, 13 females and 9 males.

Article Title: Quote of the day by The Notorious B.I.G: 'Stay far from timid, only make moves when your heart’s in it...' and the 1997 Brooklyn strategy for relentless success
Article Text:
The Notorious B.I.G.

“Stay far from timid, only make moves when your heart’s in it, and live the phrase ‘the sky’s the limit.’”

Recorded in the shadow of tragedy

The basic psychology of motivation

Applying the three rules to real life

In 1997, a young artist stood in a studio in Trinidad recording vocals for what would become one of the most famous posthumous albums in music history. He was twenty-four years old, already a giant figure in hip-hop, and balancing the pressure of massive fame alongside real danger in his industry. During these sessions, Christopher Wallace, known globally as The Notorious B.I.G., delivered a single line that summed up his entire approach to life:The line appears on the track Sky’s the Limit, featuring the R&B group 112, from Wallace’s double album Life After Death. In plain words, the advice breaks down into three simple rules: do not let fear hold you back, only do things you genuinely care about, and refuse to put limits on what you can achieve. Instead of treating success as a matter of luck, the quote presents progress as something you build through clear choices, focus, and brave action.Wallace grew up on Fulton Street in Brooklyn, New York, during the height of the 1980s crack epidemic. After starting out as a street-level dealer, his sharp rhythm and storytelling talent caught the attention of Bad Boy Records, founded by Sean "Puffy" Combs. His 1994 debut album, Ready to Die, turned him into an international star, but it also placed him at the center of a dangerous East Coast versus West Coast hip-hop rivalry.By late 1996 and early 1997, Wallace was finishing his second album. The song Sky’s the Limit was built around a sample from Bobby Caldwell’s 1978 soul hit What You Won't Do for Love, giving the track a warm, thoughtful sound. In his lyrics, Wallace shared his personal journey from growing up poor to achieving wealth, using his own life story to encourage listeners facing hard times.On March 9, 1997, just sixteen days before Life After Death was released, Wallace was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles. When the album arrived in stores on March 25, Sky’s the Limit quickly became a key track for fans grieving his loss. The song’s music video, directed by Spike Jonze, featured child actors playing Wallace and his friends inside a luxurious house, reinforcing the idea that big dreams can start in humble neighborhoods.The ideas in Wallace’s lyric match basic principles of human psychology and ancient philosophy. His warning to avoid being timid matches early thoughts about courage. Long ago, the ancient Greek thinker Aristotle wrote that true courage sits right between being too afraid and being reckless. For Aristotle, hesitating out of fear keeps a person from reaching their true potential. Wallace's call to avoid timidity asks people to take that same active, confident approach to life.In a similar way, the rule to act only when "your heart's in it" reflects what modern psychologists call intrinsic motivation. In 1985, researchers Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan developed Self-Determination Theory. Their work showed that people perform much better and feel happier over time when their actions come from real personal interest rather than outside pressure or money.When someone works solely for outside approval or cash, their drive disappears as soon as things get tough. By telling people to wait for genuine interest before making a move, Wallace described the exact mindset needed to stick with hard goals over a long period.In daily life and career planning, Wallace's three rules offer a practical test for deciding what to do next. Second-guessing yourself often leads to missed chances in school, work, and creative projects. Acting without timidity does not mean taking foolish risks; it simply means picking a goal and working toward it without letting self-doubt slow you down.The second rule helps you protect your limited time and energy. When people take on projects just out of habit or fear of saying no, the results are usually weak. Following Wallace's advice means turning down offers that do not line up with your values, saving your energy for work that truly matters to you.Finally, living the phrase "the sky's the limit" requires breaking down self-imposed mental walls. In 1954, British runner Roger Bannister ran a mile in under four minutes, breaking a record that experts had long claimed was physically impossible for human beings. Within two years, dozens of other runners ran sub-four-minute miles simply because the mental belief that it was impossible had been removed.The Notorious B.I.G. died at the young age of twenty-four, leaving behind music and ideas that continue to influence artists and listeners decades later. His advice stays relevant because it treats ambition not as a vague wish, but as a daily practice built on confidence, heart, and self-belief.
Article Summary: Christopher Wallace, known as The Notorious B.I.G., was killed in a drive-by shooting in 1997. His song Sky’s the Limit was built around a sample from Bobby Caldwell's 1978 soul hit What You Won't Do for Love. In his lyrics, Wallace shared his personal journey from growing up poor to achieving wealth.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Tupac Shakur: 'Death is not the greatest loss in life. The greatest loss is...' and the 1979 literary mystery behind hip-hop’s most unshakeable battle cry
Article Text:
Tupac Shakur

“Death is not the greatest loss in life. The greatest loss is what dies inside while still alive. Never surrender”.

Origins, misattribution, and a merged legacy

"Never surrender".

The psychology behind inner defeat

Guarding against everyday burnout

An individual can wake up every morning, commute to work, scroll through their phone, and talk with friends while quietly giving up on their curiosity, passion, and self-belief. The body keeps breathing, but the inner drive that once pushed them forward has gone cold.This quiet, internal surrender is the heart of a famous modern saying:Physical death is an unavoidable natural fact. It brings a person's life to an end, but it does so as a normal rule of nature. In contrast, losing your inner spirit happens while you are still here to live with the consequences. The quote draws a clear line between simply staying alive and truly living. It warns that cynicism, defeat, and emotional numbness are far more harmful than physical death, because they strip away meaning while a person is still breathing.On social media and quote websites, these words are almost always credited to the late rap icon Tupac Shakur. However, the first part of the statement actually belongs to the American author, editor, and peace activist Norman Cousins.Cousins wrote the original line in the 1970s while studying human resilience and healing. In his 1979 book Anatomy of an Illness as Perceived by the Patient, Cousins wrote that "death is not the greatest loss in life; the greatest loss is what dies inside us while we live". Cousins developed this view after being diagnosed with a painful, rare illness. He chose to fight his condition with humor, a positive mindset, and active self-care instead of giving in to despair.The version often shared today combines Cousins' written words with Tupac Shakur's rap message. Throughout his short life in the 1990s, Shakur wrote about the harsh reality of poverty, street violence, and unfair social systems. Songs like Keep Ya Head Up and Me Against the World urged listeners to keep fighting no matter how hard life got. Over time, internet users merged Cousins' observation with Shakur’s favorite phrase:While this combines two completely different people from different eras, the central message remains the same.The idea that losing your spirit is worse than physical death stretches back across centuries. In ancient Rome, the emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius wrote in his journal Meditations that a person should fear never starting to live far more than they fear dying. Centuries later, psychologist Viktor Frankl noticed the same thing in Nazi concentration camps. In his 1946 book Man’s Search for Meaning, Frankl observed that when a prisoner lost hope in the future, their body gave up soon after.Modern psychology explains how this inner loss happens. In 1967, American psychologist Martin Seligman discovered a pattern he called "learned helplessness." In his experiments, when people or animals were repeatedly exposed to painful events they could not control, they stopped trying to change their situation entirely. Even when the bad situation ended and an easy exit opened up, they stayed put because they believed they were powerless.When a person learns to feel helpless, their goals, hope, and joy slowly fade. They become passive observers in their own lives. This state of emotional numbness is what the quote calls the greatest loss. Physical death happens in a single moment, but losing your inner spirit is a quiet loss that you have to live through every day.This warning matters just as much today. Modern work demands, constant online scrolling, and money worries frequently leave people feeling completely drained.The World Health Organization recognizes burnout as an official work-related condition. Its main symptoms include constant exhaustion, feeling detached or negative about work, and losing confidence in your abilities. Burnout is what happens when excitement and purpose die inside someone while they keep showing up at their desk every morning.Stopping this loss requires active, everyday choices. Putting the phrase "never surrender" into practice means protecting your time, mental energy, and personal values. It shows when a worker chooses to leave a toxic job that demands they give up their self-respect. It shows when an artist keeps painting despite rejection, or when someone goes to therapy to heal old wounds instead of staying emotionally numb.Keeping your inner fire alive takes constant effort. Outside forces can take away wealth, jobs, or comfort, but losing your spirit only happens if you give up on yourself. The lasting power of the quote lies in its simple message: as long as you are breathing, the choice to care, stay curious, and keep fighting remains in your hands.
Article Summary: "Death is not the greatest loss in life. The greatest loss is what dies inside while still alive. Never surrender" is a quote from American author, editor, and peace activist Norman Cousins. The version often shared today combines Cousins' written words with Tupac Shakur's rap message.

Article Title: 'Illegally occupied': Indian Embassy in US slams foreign media for misleading headline over PoK killings
Article Text: NEW DELHI: The Indian Embassy on Wednesday criticised The New York Times for a misleading headline regarding the killings in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), asserting that Pakistan has unlawfully occupied parts of Jammu and Kashmir In a post on X, the embassy said: "Misleading and incorrect headline by The New York Times. There is no Pakistani Kashmir, only Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.""The Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh have been, are and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India. Pakistan has illegally occupied parts of these territories and is now using violence against the occupied people," it added.The criticism came after a New York Times report on violent clashes in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.According to the report, citing local officials and independent estimates, at least 30 people, including protesters, law enforcement personnel and bystanders, have been killed in clashes since early June, including in the latest round of violence on Monday.The Joint Awami Action Committee, a coalition of activist groups, has been leading protests in PoK since last month over 12 contentious seats in the so-called regional legislative assembly. The group alleges that the Pakistani establishment manipulates these seats to install a prime minister of its choice.India has maintained that the ongoing protests in PoK are "the direct consequences of Pakistan's economic exploitation, its denial of the people's fundamental rights, and its administrative oppression."
Article Summary: The Indian Embassy has criticised The New York Times for a misleading headline regarding the killings in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. At least 30 people, including protesters, law enforcement personnel and bystanders, have been killed in clashes since early June. The Joint Awami Action Committee has been leading protests in PoK since last month.
