Article Title: In 1935, the US Army dropped bombs on Hawaii’s Mauna Loa volcano hoping to divert a deadly lava flow away from Hilo
Article Text:
1935 Lava Bombing Mission: US drops 40 bombs on Mauna Loa flow

The Eruption That Threatened Hilo's Water Supply

Pāhoehoe Lava And The Science Behind The Plan

George Patton And The 40 Bombs Dropped On Mauna Loa

Why Scientists Still Disagree About What Actually Worked

On December 27, 1935, something unusual happened in the skies above Hawaiʻi. US military aircraft dropped 40 bombs, not on an enemy, but on a river of molten lava pouring down the slopes of Mauna Loa. The eruption had begun a month earlier inside the volcano's summit caldera, and by late December, a fast-moving lava flow was heading straight for Hilo and the water supply that fed it. Officials were desperate. Scientists believed that explosives could break apart the underground channels carrying lava toward the town, forcing it to spread out and slow down. What followed became one of the earliest recorded attempts at lava flow diversion, and a story still argued over nearly a century later.The Mauna Loa eruption started on November 21, 1935, inside the volcano's summit caldera. Within days, activity shifted down the Northeast Rift Zone, and a new vent opened on the volcano's northern flank on November 27. From this vent, smooth pāhoehoe lava began collecting in the saddle area between Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea before turning east toward Hilo. According to the US Geological Survey , the flow was advancing at roughly one mile a day, which put the Wailuku River, and the town's water source, directly in its path.Thomas A. Jaggar, who had founded the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, and fellow volcanologist Ruy Finch came up with an unconventional idea. They proposed using aerial bombing to rupture the lava channels near the vent itself. The goal was never to stop the eruption or destroy the lava outright. It was to break the insulated tubes and channels that let molten rock travel long distances without cooling, so the lava would spread thin across a wider area instead of racing toward Hilo in one concentrated stream.Pāhoehoe lava has a smooth, rope-like surface that cools quickly on the outside. But underneath that hardened crust, liquid lava can keep flowing through tubes and channels, insulated from the air and barely losing heat. This is exactly what allows a flow to travel for miles without solidifying. Jaggar and Finch reasoned that if bombs could tear open these channels, the lava would lose its protective covering, cool faster, and stall before reaching the river.It was not a brand new idea. Explosives had actually been proposed to stop lava flows threatening Hilo back in 1880 and 1881, though neither plan was carried out. The National Park Service describes the 1935 mission as the first time an active lava flow was ever bombed from the air anywhere in the world.Overseeing the operation was Lieutenant Colonel George S. Patton, who would go on to lead US forces during the Second World War. Aircraft flew out from Oʻahu to the Humuʻula flow and released their payload near the lava channels on Mauna Loa's northern flank. The mission used 20 demolition bombs and 20 smaller marker bombs meant to help pilots find their targets. Each demolition bomb weighed 600 pounds and packed 355 pounds of TNT, fitted with a short delay fuse so it could punch through the surface before exploding underneath.Of the demolition bombs, 16 reached the intended area, and 12 struck the lava tunnel they were aiming for. Jaggar watched the entire operation through a telescope positioned near Mauna Kea. He later called it a clear success, saying the results matched exactly what he had expected. The lava flow slowed down after the bombing and stopped completely by January 2, 1936.Not everyone was convinced. Howard Stearns, a USGS geologist who had flown along on the final bombing run, wrote in his 1983 autobiography that he believed the whole thing was simply a coincidence. The lava had kept moving even after the explosions, gradually losing strength over several days rather than stopping abruptly because of the bombs.This is really the heart of the debate. The eruption was already fading naturally around the same time the bombing took place, which makes it almost impossible to separate what the explosives actually did from what would have happened anyway. The USGS itself describes the effectiveness of using bombs to break lava channels as unresolved. A second bombing attempt in 1942 produced similarly unclear results.What the 1935 mission does represent, regardless of how one reads the outcome, is one of the earliest organised efforts by humans to influence where lava travels rather than trying to stop a volcano altogether. Nearly ninety years on, with modern instruments and far better understanding of how lava tubes behave, scientists are still cautious about claiming victory over something as unpredictable as an active volcano. Mauna Loa, it turns out, keeps its own counsel.
Article Summary: US dropped 40 bombs on a river of molten lava pouring down the slopes of Mauna Loa. The lava flow was heading straight for Hilo and the water supply that fed it. Scientists believed that explosives could break apart the underground channels carrying lava toward the town, forcing it to spread out.

Article Title: Anthony Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment at Senate hearing on Covid response
Article Text:
Dr Anthony Fauci

Clash with senator Rand Paul over pandemic response





Research funding dispute





Political fallout, records, defence





Former US Chief Medical Advisor Dr Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment during a Republican-led Senate hearing on Wednesday, declining to answer questions about his role in the federal COVID-19 response after being subpoenaed to appear.Fauci, who led the nation’s pandemic response, said he was acting on legal advice and described the decision as difficult. His refusal to testify immediately escalated tensions in an already highly charged political dispute over the origins and management of the coronavirus pandemic.The hearing was requested by Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has repeatedly accused Fauci of misleading Congress about COVID-19’s origins and the US government’s involvement in related research.In his opening statement, Fauci accused Paul of pursuing a political campaign aimed at securing his prosecution.“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this Committee is to prompt me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said.Paul, in turn, alleged that Fauci helped fund virus research that contributed to the pandemic and later attempted to obscure his involvement.“Instead of an apology, you have for years avoided responsibility,” Paul said.A central focus of the hearing was US-funded research conducted through EcoHealth Alliance in collaboration with a laboratory in Wuhan, China. Republican lawmakers have suggested this research may have played a role in the emergence of COVID-19.Fauci has previously rejected claims of wrongdoing, stating that the research funded by the National Institutes of Health did not involve the type of high-risk gain-of-function experiments critics allege. He has also said that while he considered multiple theories, the strongest evidence still supports a natural origin of the virus.Most scientists continue to believe COVID-19 likely emerged naturally from animals before spreading to humans, though the lab-leak theory remains politically contentious. A Republican-led congressional subcommittee in 2024 did not find evidence linking Fauci to misconduct.Ahead of the hearing, Senator Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary entries from the pandemic period, claiming they contradicted Fauci’s public statements. Some entries reflecting early uncertainty about the virus had already been disclosed in Fauci’s memoir and prior interviews.The hearing drew criticism from Democrats, with Senator Gary Peters calling it a partisan exercise focused on past disputes rather than current policy concerns.Fauci’s attorney, David Schertler, dismissed the allegations as “false and disgraceful” and said legal options were being considered. Meanwhile, more than 150 scientists signed a letter defending Fauci, stating that “no credible evidence has been produced” to support the accusations and urging Congress to end what they called “witch-hunts.”
Article Summary: Former US Chief Medical Advisor Dr Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment during a Republican-led Senate hearing on Wednesday. The hearing was requested by Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has repeatedly accused F Kauci of misleading Congress about COVID-19’s origins and the US government's involvement in related research.

Article Title: California researchers surveyed Point Reyes lagoon 19 times and found 73 pelicans killed by river otters; some birds have now begun flying away when otters approach
Article Text:
These otters are not part of the study. (Image Credit: Harry Collins Photography/Shutterstock)

Regular counts show high pelican deaths

High energy needs lead to surprising food choice

Pelicans start showing signs of escape

Field observations reveal ecological impact

Wildlife researchers checking the shores of Abbotts Lagoon on California’s Point Reyes peninsula found 73 dead brown pelicans killed by river otters over 19 visits. Recent observations show that the large seabirds may finally be learning to fly away when otters come near.The findings, published in a study in the IUCN Otter Specialist Group Bulletin and reported by Discover Magazine, show a rare hunting relationship between two animal groups that are recovering in numbers in Northern California.Researchers Terence Carroll and Megan Isadore, co-founders of the River Otter Ecology Project, led the study. They first saw an attack at Abbotts Lagoon in October 2021, watching an otter drag a pelican with a six-foot wingspan underwater to drown it. Visitors, photos, and videos had shown similar attacks since late 2018, but no formal study had measured how often they happened.To measure the hunting, Carroll and Isadore walked the shoreline every 7 to 10 days from June to November 2023. On each trip, they mapped where they found dead pelicans and marked their bones so no bird was counted twice.The team found fresh dead birds on 17 out of their 19 visits, counting as many as 11 dead pelicans in one trip.The researchers noted that the true number of deaths was likely higher, as scavengers often carry away bodies and parts of the shore are hard to reach.According to the study, river otters leave a clear mark on the birds they hunt. Otters usually bite off the pelicans' heads and necks to get to the meat on the chest. This feeding style helped Carroll and Isadore confirm otter kills even when they did not see the attack happen.Data from the bird-watching website eBird showed that dead bird numbers went up during weeks when larger groups of pelicans gathered at Abbotts Lagoon, likely leaving lone birds exposed along the edges of the flock.While river otters eat fish and smaller water birds all year, hunting a large bird that weighs 3 to 4 kilograms takes a lot of work.The researchers noted that an earlier report on similar attacks at Rodeo Lagoon thought bad water quality had reduced fish numbers, forcing otters to hunt pelicans instead. However, Carroll and Isadore found no water quality problems at Abbotts Lagoon.Instead, the study suggests this hunting is a natural extension of how otters usually find food. Swimming in cold water makes otters burn energy and lose body heat quickly, making big, slow-moving birds sitting on the water an easy meal. A pelican gives the otter plenty of food that it can pull onto dry land to eat.Both species are conservation success stories in the area. Brown pelicans were taken off the US federal endangered species list in 2009, while river otters have been returning to their old habitats across Northern California.Early survey results from 2023 showed that pelicans made no effort to stay away from dangerous spots. Groups kept resting in areas where fresh dead birds lay along the shore.However, visits in late summer 2024 showed a possible change in how the birds react to the swimming predators. While checking a spot where they found about 20 dead birds in 2023, Carroll and Isadore found only three.During these later trips, the researchers watched resting pelicans fly away as soon as an otter swam towards them. Another watcher recorded the exact same escape behaviour at Rodeo Lagoon in August 2024.Beyond the direct mortality count, the study published in the IUCN Otter Specialist Group Bulletin details how otter attacks ripple through the local coastal food chain.When otters kill brown pelicans, they eat only specific body parts, mainly the breast muscle, and leave behind substantial portions of the heavy bird carcasses on the banks. Researchers noted that these leftovers act as a new food supply for local land-based scavengers.Field data recorded coyotes repeatedly visiting the lagoon banks to feed on the remains left behind by otters. In several instances, cameras captured coyotes actively taking pelican carcasses straight from otters.This interaction shows that river otters are moving energy and nutrients from marine and lagoon waters onto dry land, creating a fresh nutrient link between aquatic and terrestrial wildlife at Point Reyes National Seashore.Survey records also show that these attacks happen during specific times of the year. Pelican deaths peak between late summer and autumn, matching the seasonal migration pattern when brown pelicans travel north along the Pacific coast to gather in Northern California estuaries.Despite the high death toll of 73 birds recorded in 2023, wildlife surveys confirm that the overall population of brown pelicans at Point Reyes remains stable.The attacks do not threaten the species as a whole, but they represent a rare, documented case of two recovering native species adapting to each other in shared waters.
Article Summary: Researchers found 73 dead brown pelicans killed by river otters over 19 visits to Abbotts Lagoon on California’s Point Reyes peninsula. Otters usually bite off the pelicans' heads and necks to get to the meat on the chest. Researchers noted that these leftovers act as a new food supply for local land scavengers.

Article Title: 'They are the main culprits': US Senator on bill that imposes up to 100% tariffs on India, China
Article Text:
US Senator Richard Blumenthal. (Photo: X)

'Let's be blunt': India, China are 'main culprits'

Claims tariffs curbed India's Russian oil imports

Bill would allow tariffs of up to 100 %

India has defended Russian oil purchases

US Senator Richard Blumenthal defended proposed legislation that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, saying the measure is designed to target countries such as India and China rather than US allies.Speaking after the Senate advanced the bipartisan bill, Blumenthal accused India and China of helping finance Russia's war in Ukraine through their energy purchases.He also claimed that tariffs imposed by the Trump administration had already led India to significantly reduce its imports of Russian crude.Blumenthal said the legislation does not mandate tariffs but authorises the president to impose duties of up to 100 per cent on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas."The bill doesn't require tariffs. It authorizes tariffs up to 100 per cent to the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas. It's carefully crafted to make sure we are not hitting our allies and that we are hitting China and India."He added: "Let's be really blunt. China and India are the main culprits here. They purchase the vast majority of oil and gas. They are fueling Russia's war machine, and they are doing us no favors anywhere else in the world."Blumenthal argued that tariffs and sanctions have already had an impact, pointing to India's oil trade with Russia."The president imposed tariffs of about 25 per cent on India, and they cut their purchases of Russian oil by 50 per cent."He maintained that economic pressure can influence countries' behaviour."Tariffs and sanctions have consequences, and the president is gonna be under a lot of pressure to use them, and he is signing this bill with the expectation publicly that he will use them."The bipartisan legislation would authorise Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on imports from countries that continue purchasing substantial quantities of Russian oil and gas.It also proposes sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions and the so-called shadow fleet used to bypass existing restrictions on Russian oil exports, while expanding measures linked to Iran.The proposal must still clear additional Senate votes before moving to the House of Representatives.India remains one of the world's largest buyers of Russian crude and is second only to China in imports.Russian oil has become a major part of India's energy basket since the Ukraine war, with refiners increasing purchases of discounted crude to meet domestic demand.According to commodities data firm Kpler, India imported a record 2.7 million barrels per day of Russian crude in June and about 2.6 million barrels per day during the first three weeks of July, accounting for more than half of the country's total crude imports.New Delhi has repeatedly defended the purchases, saying its energy imports are guided by affordability, availability and national energy security rather than geopolitical considerations.Last month, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said the US had previously encouraged India to buy Russian oil to help stabilise global energy markets after sanctions disrupted supplies, while Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri has maintained that India has never been asked to halt imports from Russia
Article Summary: Bill would allow tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. Senator Richard Blumenthal says measure is designed to target countries such as India and China rather than US allies. He claims tariffs imposed by the Trump administration had already led India to significantly reduce its imports of Russian crude.
